summary.text: The universal formulation includes \(n=0\); under the stipulated extension of the divisor sums and totient, \(a(0)=0\). Since \(0\neq1\) and \(0\) is not prime, this contradicts the asserted characterization of the zero values.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
D(n)=\{d\in\mathbb N:1\le d<n+1\text{ and }d\mid n\}.
\]
Thus, for positive \(n\), \(D(n)\) is the usual finite set of positive divisors of \(n\). The definition used in the statement extends this to \(n=0\) by the same bounded-set formula. Define
\[
\sigma_1(n)=\sum_{d\in D(n)}d,
\qquad
\sigma_2(n)=\sum_{d\in D(n)}d^2,
\]
and let \(\varphi(n)\) be the number of natural numbers \(r<n\) that are coprime to \(n\). Finally, if \(z\) is an integer, write
\[
z_{\ge0}=\max(z,0),
\]
which is the conversion from an integer to a natural number used in the definition. The function in the proposed theorem is therefore
\[
a(n)=\bigl(\sigma_2(n)+\varphi(n)\sigma_1(n)-2n^2\bigr)_{\ge0}.
\]

The proposition to be disproved quantifies over every natural number \(n\), with no assumption \(n\ge1\), and asserts in particular
\[
a(n)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad n=1\text{ or }n\text{ is prime}.
\tag{1}
\]
It also asserts a second biconditional characterizing \(a(n)=2\), but it is enough to contradict (1).

Take \(n=0\). We calculate every term in the definition of \(a(0)\). By the definition of \(D(n)\), an element of \(D(0)\) would have to satisfy
\[
1\le d<0+1=1.
\]
No natural number does so. Hence
\[
D(0)=\varnothing.
\]
Both divisor sums are consequently empty sums, and therefore
\[
\sigma_1(0)=0,
\qquad
\sigma_2(0)=0.
\]
Likewise, there is no natural number \(r<0\). The set counted by the totient at zero is empty, so
\[
\varphi(0)=0.
\]
Also \(2\cdot0^2=0\). Substitution gives
\[
\sigma_2(0)+\varphi(0)\sigma_1(0)-2\cdot0^2
 =0+0\cdot0-0
 =0.
\]
Taking the nonnegative part leaves zero unchanged. Thus
\[
a(0)=0.
\tag{2}
\]

Now suppose, for contradiction, that the universally quantified proposed statement were true. Applying its first biconditional (1) at \(n=0\), and using (2), would imply
\[
0=1\quad\text{or}\quad 0\text{ is prime}.
\tag{3}
\]
There are two cases in this disjunction, and each is impossible. The first, \(0=1\), is false because zero and one are distinct natural numbers. The second is also false: every prime natural number is at least \(2\), whereas \(0<2\). Equivalently, zero cannot satisfy the defining condition for primality.

Thus both alternatives in (3) are false, contradicting the consequence of the proposed biconditional. Therefore the conjunction claimed by the theorem cannot hold for every natural number. In particular,
\[
\neg\,\forall n\in\mathbb N,\;
\left[
\bigl(a(n)=0\leftrightarrow n=1\lor n\text{ is prime}\bigr)
\land
\bigl(a(n)=2\leftrightarrow
\exists p,q\; (p,q\text{ prime},\ p\ne q,\ n=pq)\bigr)
\right].
\]
The second biconditional requires no analysis, since the first one already fails at \(n=0\).

This counterexample exploits the precise domain of the proposition: it ranges over all natural numbers, although the OEIS sequence and the canonical conjecture begin at \(n=1\). Accordingly, the argument disproves the stated universal formal proposition, which omitted the hypothesis \(n\ge1\); it does not supply a counterexample among the positive integers and hence does not, by itself, refute the intended positive-domain OEIS assertion.
